analysis.one_liner: Bans emergency oil reserve sales to China and embargoed countries while requiring expanded federal oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never left its four House committees, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban selling oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve — the government's emergency stockpile — to countries under U.S. arms embargoes, state sponsors of terrorism, or any Chinese-owned company. Before any reserve drawdown, the Energy Department would have to produce a plan to lease a matching share more federal land for oil and gas drilling. It would also rescind President Biden's executive order on climate and public health and order every federal agency to repeal rules that curb 'energy independence' and write new rules to boost energy producers' output.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: more federal land and seabed leased for drilling whenever the reserve is tapped, rescission of the climate executive order that guides federal permitting, and a directive to every agency to lighten their regulatory burden. The export ban itself is narrow — it covers only barrels sold from the reserve, not the industry's broader export business.

how_it_helps.text: Before any first drawdown of reserve oil by sale, exchange, or loan, the Energy Secretary must develop a plan to increase the share of federal land leased for oil and gas production by the same percentage as the drawdown.

On the date of enactment, the President must rescind Executive Order 13990, the Biden administration's order directing agencies to consider climate and public-health effects, and order agencies to repeal rules reducing 'energy independence' and to reduce the regulatory burden on energy producers.

The Energy Secretary must bar exporting reserve oil sold to arms-embargoed countries, state sponsors of terrorism, or any entity wholly or partially owned by China — the bill's findings state that 2022 emergency sales were bought by Unipec, a subsidiary of Chinese oil firm Sinopec.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost of weakened environmental review: rescinding the climate executive order reverses the government's use of climate and health criteria in federal decisions, and agencies could repeal pollution safeguards under the open-ended 'energy independence' directive. There is no guaranteed price relief for consumers, since oil is priced in a global market.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via weaker environmental rules

drawbacks.text: Rescinding Executive Order 13990 would reverse climate and public-health criteria across federal agencies, including environmental review of fossil-fuel projects.
Requiring a federal-land leasing plan before each reserve drawdown could slow or complicate emergency oil sales at the moment they are most needed, which is the reserve's core purpose.
Directing agencies to repeal any regulation with the 'intent or effect' of reducing energy independence is open-ended and could sweep in pollution and safety rules with no offsetting protections.
The export ban covers only barrels sold from the reserve, a small share of petroleum trade, so its effect on consumer prices would be limited even though it is the bill's headline provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The export restriction responds to a documented, unpopular practice — emergency reserve oil ending up with a Chinese subsidiary — and most people would support keeping emergency stockpiles at home. But that is the small part of the bill. Its larger provisions condition emergency drawdowns on new drilling leases and roll back the administration's climate and regulatory framework for the benefit of producers, without a reliable mechanism for lowering prices at the pump. On balance, the bill trades modest, real public benefits for a broad deregulation agenda whose costs fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2022 with no cosponsors, referred to four House committees and then two subcommittees, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot introduced the bill on September 2, 2022 as the sole sponsor.
No member of the House from either party cosponsored the bill.

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Natural Resources, and Oversight committees, then to the Energy and Railroads subcommittees, and received no further action.
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee, so it never came to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing climate executive order and regulatory framework stayed in place, and oil and gas producers got no new federal leasing mandate. On the other side, reserve sales remained unrestricted, so Chinese-owned buyers could keep purchasing emergency oil.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Climate rules stayed; reserve sales stayed open

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsor was a House Republican; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would condition every reserve drawdown on leasing proportionally more federal land for drilling, rescind the climate executive order, and order agencies to cut industry regulation. In exchange it bars reserve sales only to China-owned buyers, leaving the industry's broader export freedom untouched. The deregulation and leasing gains run against public environmental interests; the export ban's stated aim of keeping emergency oil home runs with them.

The bill's findings state 2022 emergency reserve sales were purchased by Unipec, a Sinopec subsidiary, and delivered to China; the ban would end that access. Its loss tracks the public's gain under the bill's own national-security logic.

The bill's sense of Congress endorses producing 'all available energy sources, including coal,' and its deregulation directives cover energy producers broadly, which would ease rules on coal alongside oil and gas. That gain comes at the expense of air-quality and climate protections the public relies on.
